sentences.text: This creature was first described in 1992 as a skeleton measuring roughly the size of a sparrow.
Its remains show a mix of ancient traits and modern bird characteristics.
The hands held moderately curved claws that were not as sharply bent as those seen in Archaeopteryx.
Like the famous transitional fossil Archaeopteryx, the pubis bone pointed downward and ended in a hook-like shape.
The front limbs possessed separate wrist and hand bones, unlike the fused structures found in living birds.
The pelvic region included a pubis bone that supported a foot.
Evidence suggests this animal could perch on branches and climb trees.
It had separate finger bones for flight and a shortened tail that moved the body's center of gravity forward.
Scientists initially estimated the fossil was about 135 million years old.
Subsequent studies adjusted the age of the rock layers to between 120 and 110 million years.
Its anatomy indicates it shared flight and perching skills with modern sparrows living in trees.
This bird belongs to the subclass known as Enantiornithes.
It is classified within the broader group Reptilia.
In 2001, researchers Paul Sereno and colleagues suggested the species Cathayornis was a junior synonym of Sinornis.
It lived during the Lower Cretaceous period in the Jiufotang Formation of China.
Specific dating places it in the Aptian stage, between 121.4 and 113.2 million years ago.
In 2001, Zhou and Hou argued that Cathayornis and Sinornis are distinct genera, citing differences in size, finger structure, and claw length.
They further distinguished the two based on the larger size of Cathayornis, a shorter and straighter first digit with a slightly longer claw, and the absence of an atitrocánter.
